# Create PR

Create a pull request for the committed work on the current branch. Use this
skill when the user asks to create or open a GitHub pull request; do not use it
merely to draft a PR title or description.

## Inspect before mutating

1. Inspect the current branch, worktree, remotes, and commits relative to the
   target branch. The target is the branch explicitly named by the user;
   otherwise use `main`.
2. Require a clean worktree and committed changes. Do not create, amend, or
   rewrite commits as part of this skill.
3. Verify that the target branch exists on `origin` and that the current branch
   is not the target branch.
4. Run `gh auth status` to confirm GitHub CLI logins exist, then select the
   account that matches the repository (see [Account selection](#account-selection)).
   Use that account for every GitHub action; never request, set, expose, or
   change credentials.
5. Check whether a pull request already exists from the current branch into the
   target branch, using the selected account and an explicit `--repo`. If it
   does, return its URL rather than creating a duplicate.

## Account selection

A single `gh` install can hold several logged-in accounts, and `gh` uses the
globally active one regardless of the repository. When accounts differ per
organization this can create the pull request under the wrong identity, or fail
when the active account cannot access the repository. SSH routing (via remote
host aliases) does not carry over to `gh`, which talks to the API over HTTPS.

Select the correct account per repository instead of relying on the active one:

1. Resolve the `owner/repo` slug from `git remote get-url origin`, stripping any
   SSH host alias (handle both `git@<alias>:owner/repo.git` and HTTPS forms).
2. List the logged-in accounts from `gh auth status`.
3. Pick the account whose token can reach the repository. For each account,
   probe access and use the first that succeeds:

   ```sh
   GH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token -u <account>)" gh repo view <owner>/<repo>
   ```

   When only one account is logged in, use it. When none can access the
   repository, stop and report rather than opening the pull request under the
   wrong identity.
4. Scope every `gh` command to the selected account by exporting its token for
   that command only, and pass an explicit `--repo`. This never changes the
   globally active account:

   ```sh
   GH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token -u <account>)" gh <command> --repo <owner>/<repo> ...
   ```

## Create the pull request

1. Push the current branch only when it is not already available on its remote.
   Push and create the pull request only when the user explicitly requests
   those external actions.
2. Use a Conventional Commit-style title:

   ```text
   <type>(<optional-scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Use `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `test`, `chore`, `ci`, `build`,
   `perf`, or `revert`. Omit the scope when it does not make the title clearer.
3. Draft the body from [the pull-request template](references/pull-request-template.md).
   Remove unused bullets. Add a `Notes` section only for a review-relevant
   limitation, migration, decision, or follow-up.
4. Create the PR with the selected account, an explicit base branch, and an
   explicit repository, for example:

   ```sh
   GH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token -u <account>)" \
     gh pr create --repo <owner>/<repo> --base <target-branch> ...
   ```

5. Return the PR URL, source branch, target branch, and verification performed.

## Identity and attribution

GitHub attributes the PR to the selected `gh` account. Do not set or alter Git
author or committer identity. Do not add `Co-authored-by`, `Assisted-by`, AI
attribution, or equivalent attribution to commits, PR titles, or PR bodies.
